text:
When a vehicle drives onto a suspension bridge, its weight immediately joins the massive dead weight of the structure itself. Carrying these combined forces from a roadway suspended high in the air down into the solid earth relies on a continuous, balanced interplay of tension and compression. The journey begins at the bridge deck, the flat surface carrying traffic. Underneath or alongside this roadway sits a rigid stiffening truss or an aerodynamic steel box girder. Without this underlying framework, the flexible deck would sag dangerously under localized weights, such as a heavy truck, or twist violently in high winds. The stiffening structure spreads these concentrated forces out evenly across a much wider section of the bridge.

From the edges of the stiffened deck, the distributed weight transfers to vertical steel ropes known as suspender cables, or hangers. Spaced at regular intervals along the span, these suspenders hold the deck aloft. Because gravity pulls the roadway downward, the suspenders are stretched tight and operate purely in tension. They carry the load straight up to the bridge's primary structural arteries: the sweeping main cables. Draped high above the water, the main cables collect the cumulative pull of every individual suspender. Because a flexible steel cable cannot resist bending, it naturally assumes a smooth parabolic curve under the uniform weight of the deck, allowing it to carry the entire burden through axial tension along its length.

As the main cables sweep upward from the center of the bridge, they channel this immense tensile force to the tops of the main towers. There, the cables rest in heavy, curved steel bearings called saddles. These saddles allow the cables to slide minutely as traffic loads shift and temperatures change, ensuring the tall towers are not pulled out of alignment. Because the cables slope downward on both sides of each tower, their opposing horizontal pulls balance out, translating the force into a massive vertical push straight downward. At this junction, the primary force flips from tension to compression. The towers, built of thick cellular steel or reinforced concrete, act as giant vertical columns. They absorb this crushing downward weight and channel it down into deep foundations, or piers, which transfer the load directly into solid bedrock beneath the water or soil.

Yet the towers alone cannot complete the load path. The heavy central span pulls inward on the cables with a tremendous force that would easily topple the towers toward the center of the crossing if left unchecked. To counter this inward pull, the main cables continue past the towers, sloping down to the shorelines on either side to enter massive concrete blocks or natural rock formations called anchorages. Inside an anchorage, each thick main cable splays out into thousands of individual steel wires, dispersing the immense tension deep within the structure. Relying either on sheer, immovable dead weight and friction with the earth, or on deep mechanical bonds with solid bedrock, the anchorages resist the relentless tug of the cables, finally grounding the last of the bridge's forces safely into the earth.
